name: Predictable Responses
description: Learn to recognize a partner’s actual response to your attack instead of assuming a reflex. Practice clear cues, two useful follow-ups, and a reset when control is lost.
summary: Useful follow-ups begin with the response you can observe, not the reaction you expected an opponent to give.
overview: A familiar attack often draws familiar defenses, but people can post, retreat, counter, or do nothing. Start with two likely responses and identify the body position that makes each follow-up available.
key_takeaways: Describe a response as a visible change: a hand posts, weight moves back, or a knee comes inside.
Treat common reactions as possibilities, not hardwired rules.
Keep using the first attack when the opponent has not stopped it.
If the expected cue is absent, keep control or rebuild instead of launching the memorized answer.
Review the response itself after a round; a failed follow-up may reflect a wrong read rather than a bad technique.

bjj_applications.scenario: Your butterfly sweep makes the opponent post a hand
bjj_applications.application: Check whether that hand remains available and whether you still control their upper body. Choose a continuation suited to those connections rather than reaching for the arm after it has already returned.
bjj_applications.outcome: The follow-up is tied to a present opening.

bjj_applications.scenario: You pull forward from closed guard and the opponent regains upright posture
bjj_applications.application: If their weight moves back and you can sit up with control, a hip-bump entry may be available. If they stay close, use the connection you have instead of forcing the sit-up.
bjj_applications.outcome: The same initial action gives information for two different decisions.

bjj_applications.scenario: A guard player turns their knees toward your passing direction
bjj_applications.application: Watch whether their hips follow and which knee can still re-enter. Change direction only while your grips and balance allow it.
bjj_applications.outcome: You respond to the defensive shape, not simply to seeing movement.

common_mistakes.mistake: Believing a push always creates a push back
common_mistakes.consequence: Some partners retreat, change angle, or attack instead.
common_mistakes.correction: Test the response at manageable intensity and prepare for more than one result.

common_mistakes.mistake: Remembering the technique name but missing the cue
common_mistakes.consequence: You attempt a valid follow-up in the wrong position.
common_mistakes.correction: State the required hand, hip, or weight change before drilling the continuation.

training_exercises.name: Two responses, unscripted
training_exercises.description: Choose a familiar guard attack. Agree on two realistic defenses, then let top choose either without announcing it. Bottom follows the actual cue; reset on a sweep, pass, lost connection, or tap.
training_exercises.focus: Separate recognizing the defense from memorizing a sequence.

training_exercises.name: Add the missing answer
training_exercises.description: Repeat the same exercise with the partner also allowed to leave the first attack available. Finish that attack when possible; stop and reset at the result.
training_exercises.focus: Avoid switching merely because you expect a defense.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your planned follow-up needs a posted hand, but the hand is already back. What now?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Do not chase the absent opening. Continue an available attack, retain your position, or rebuild the setup.

knowledge_assessment.question: What should a useful note after a round contain?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The attack you tried, the response you saw, and which control or opening was present for the next action.
